title: Bamum (Bamoun) kingdom
text:
Bamum (Bamoun) kingdom (kingdom)
Founded: 1394, by the Tikar prince Nshare Yèn (Nchare), who settled in the region and built the palace at Foumban.
Capital: Foumban, in the Noun Department of the West Region.
Title of ruler: King (mfon), a hereditary position. The ruler is also called Sultan.
Continuity: The monarchy has survived through about 20 reigns. One source calls the present king the 19th monarch.
Reigning king: Mouhammad Nabil Mforifoum Mbombo Njoya, from 2021, according to one source.
Craft: The Bamum are noted craftsmen. King Njoya's palace had 300 looms and six dye pits.
Week: King Mônjù (1461 to 1498) introduced an eight-day week.

title: King Ibrahim Njoya
text:
King Ibrahim Njoya (public figure)
Reign: 1889 to 1933
Known as: The most celebrated of the Bamum kings.
Inventions: The Bamum script (A-ka-u-ku) around 1896, the Shümom language in 1912, and a corn-grinding machine.
Religion: Founded a hybrid belief called Nwet-Nkwete, mixing Islam, Christianity and animist beliefs.
Palace: Built the Foumban palace, completed in 1917.
Exile: Exiled by the French authorities in 1931. He died in 1933.
Successor: His son Seidou Njimoluh Njoya.

title: Bamum script (A-ka-u-ku)
text:
Bamum script (A-ka-u-ku) (writing system)
Inventor: King Ibrahim Njoya, with the help of at least two royal advisers, Nji Mama Pekekue and Adjia Nji-Gboron.
Invented: Around 1895 or 1896. The first version, called Lerewa or Lewa, was completed around 1897.
Size: Over 500 syllabic signs. Britannica counts 510 pictographic characters in the first system.
Development: The script evolved through six stages between 1897 and 1931.
Use: Thousands of works were written in it, from official letters and school texts to epics and court records.
Origin story: Njoya was inspired to create writing after a revelatory dream.
Related language: The Shümom language, introduced by Njoya in 1912.

title: Foumban Royal Palace
text:
Foumban Royal Palace (building)
Location: Foumban, in the Noun Department of the West Region.
Built: 1917, under King Njoya.
Style: Shows influences from German colonial buildings.
Use: The seat of the Kingdom of Bamum, where the king still lives.
Unesco: On Cameroon's UNESCO World Heritage tentative list, since 2006 according to one source.
Museum: The palace museum tells the history of the Bamum kings from 1394 to today.

title: Museum of the Bamoun Kings
text:
Museum of the Bamoun Kings (museum)
Location: Foumban
Opened: 2024, with about 2,000 guests.
Collection: About 12,500 pieces, including weapons, pipes, musical instruments, a beaded royal stool, masks, costumes, King Njoya's manuscripts and the corn-grinding machine he invented.
Building: Construction was launched in 2013 by King Ibrahim Mbombo Njoya, because the palace rooms were too small. Only a few of the pieces had been shown in the palace before.
Entrance: Visitors pass under a large two-headed snake from the royal coat of arms.

title: doual'art
text:
doual'art (institution)
Description: An independent contemporary art centre and exhibition space in Douala.
Founded: 1991, by Princess Marilyn Douala Manga Bell and the art historian Didier Schaub.
Place: Place du Gouvernement, Bonanjo, Douala.
Main project: The SUD Salon Urbain de Douala triennial of public art.
Landmark: La Nouvelle Liberté by Joseph-Francis Sumégné, commissioned in 1996.

title: SUD Salon Urbain de Douala
text:
SUD Salon Urbain de Douala (festival)
Description: A triennial festival of public art and contemporary art in Douala, organised by doual'art.
Editions: The first was in December 2007, the second in December 2010, the third in 2013 on the theme Douala Métamorphoses, and the fourth in 2017 on the theme La place de l'Humain, dedicated to youth.
Output: Performances, installations and permanent public artworks. Counts differ: one source says more than 80 works and events, another says around sixty works.
Permanent works: Include L'Arbre à Palabres by Frédéric Keiff and Nje Mo Ye by Koko Komégné.
Impact: Douala has taken on public art projects, with monuments unveiled or renovated, thanks to SUD.

Description: A permanent monumental sculpture in recycled material, about 12 metres high with a wingspan of 5 metres.
Place: The Deïdo traffic circle in Douala.

title: Decree No. 77/245 on traditional chieftaincies
text:
Decree No. 77/245 on traditional chieftaincies (law)
Date: 15 July 1977 (one source gives 25 July)
Subject: Organises traditional chiefdoms in Cameroon.
Structure: Three classes of chiefdom: first, second and third.
Status of chiefs: Traditional chiefs are recognised as auxiliaries of the administration.
Selection: In principle, chiefs are chosen from families that customarily provide the traditional leader.
Related: Order No. 19/CAB/PM of 7 February 1981 lists the traditional chiefdoms.

title: Titles of traditional rulers
text:
Titles of traditional rulers (concept)
Titles: Depending on the region, a traditional chief may be called Fo (Fon), Mfo, Lamido, Mey or, in some Muslim chieftaincies, Sultan.
Lamido regions: Lamido is the title used in the Far North, North and Adamawa regions.
Fon region: Fon is the title used in the grassfields of the Northwest Region.
Role: A chief has both political and spiritual duties, according to a Canadian refugee board research response.

title: Lamidat
text:
Lamidat (institution)
Description: The chiefdom of the Fulani (Peulh) theocracies of the north, ruled by a lamido.
Palace: A lamido's palace has an audience hall, wall frescoes that illustrate the history of the kingdom, objects linked to the cult, and vestments, reflecting the grandeur of the lamido.
Regions: The title lamido is used in the Far North, North and Adamawa regions.
Related: See also the record on titles of traditional rulers.

title: Lamidat of Rey Bouba
text:
Lamidat of Rey Bouba (kingdom)
Place: Rey Bouba, a town in the Mayo-Rey Department of the North Region.
History: Centre of the Lamidat (sultanate) of Rey Bouba, a vassal state of the Yola (Adamawa) Emirate, which was itself a vassal of the Sokoto Caliphate.
People: The inhabitants, the Boubandjidda, were of Hausa-Fulani origin.
Palace: The Palace of Rey Bouba is the seat of the lamidat and is built in local mud-brick architecture.
Heritage: Entered in the UNESCO World Heritage tentative list as Le Lamidat de Rey-Bouba, and on Cameroon's indicative list of cultural heritage.
First ruler: French Wikipedia names Bouba Ndjidda as the first known ruler and says he came from the region of Mali.

title: Mandara Kingdom (Wandala)
text:
Mandara Kingdom (Wandala) (kingdom)
Emergence: A more centralised state emerged around the Mandara Mountains in northern Cameroon at the end of the 1400s.
Names: Sometimes called the Mandara Kingdom and sometimes the Wandala.
Decline: It declined when Fulani people invaded in a jihad.
Fulani relations: The relationship was complicated: Mandara kings sometimes invited Fulani warriors to protect them from internal threats, so Fulani influence was large long before the final Fulani conquest in 1893.
Related heritage: The Diy-Gid-Biy Cultural Landscape of the Mandara Mountains was inscribed on the World Heritage List in July 2025.

title: Fulani expansion into Adamawa
text:
Fulani expansion into Adamawa (history)
Late 18th century: One account says a group of Fulani advanced south of Lake Chad in the late 18th century, drove people into the Mandara Mountains, and set up about sixty small emirates in the upland region that became known as Adamawa.
Other dating: The US State Department dates the Fulani conquest of most of northern Cameroon to between the late 1770s and the early 1800s.
Caution: Sources give different dates and details.

title: Traditional dress in Cameroon
text:
Traditional dress in Cameroon (overview)
Cultural areas: Traditional dress is usually described by four cultural areas: Fang-Beti-Bulu, Sawa, Grassfields and Soudano-Sahelian.
Regional outfits: Ndop (Bamileke), tiè-yàa (Bamoun), toghu (Northwest) and kaba ngondo (Littoral).
Spread: Outfits once tied to specific peoples have spread nationwide. Batik, formerly the ritual dress of the Bamileke, Bamoun and Bamenda peoples in the west, is now worn by all Cameroonians and in the diaspora. The kaba ngondo, from the Littoral, has become a national outfit.
Wax and pagne: Loincloth fabrics (bazin, wax, serrated) have origins in the Far North, after woven fabrics (leppi). Wax is the most widely used.

Toghu (garment)
Also spelled: Atoghu, Tugh, teghou
Origin: Bamenda and the grassfields of the Northwest Region.
Description: An embroidered velvet outfit, often a sleeveless vest.
Past use: Once reserved for royalty and dignitaries.
Now: Widely worn at ceremonies and by Cameroonians abroad.

title: Ndop
text:
Ndop (textile)
Also called: Ndep, nze dop
Origin: Grassfields and the Bamileke Plateau of western Cameroon.
Making: Handwoven cloth that is dyed with resist techniques, often in indigo blue.
Use: A royal display cloth that sets the scene at royal ceremonies and festivals, a funerary cloth, and a favourite gift between leaders and elites.
History: The patterns are said to follow cloth from eastern and central Nigeria brought by Hausa traders.
Meaning: Symbolises wealth, power and royal privilege.

Description: A flowing maxi yoke dress.

title: Abine-mfor and Mandeleh festivals of Bafut
text:
Abine-mfor and Mandeleh festivals of Bafut (festival)
Place: Bafut Palace, the royal residence of the Fon of Bafut, in the Northwest Region.
Abine mfor: Means dance of the Fon in the Bafut language, and is also called Abine Lela, the flutes' dance.
Purpose: The Bafut people perform traditional rituals to honour ancestral spirits, reflecting their religious and political beliefs.
Timing: One charity blog says the Fon dance is held every December and has been held every year since 1516, which I could not verify.
Palace: The same blog calls Bafut Palace the centre of the region's politics and religious rites for over 400 years.
Mandeleh: A second major annual festival held at the palace.

title: Ngondo
text:
Ngondo (festival)
Type: Annual water-centred festival
People: The Sawa coastal peoples, including the Duala, Bassa, Bakoko, Bakweri and Ewodi.
Place: Douala, on the banks of the Wouri River.
Timing: December, often the first week.
Highlight: A ceremony of the jengu, a water spirit in Sawa belief.
Activities: Pirogue rituals, wrestling, swimming competitions, traditional dance and a fashion parade of Sawa regalia.
History: Established in 1949 for a commemorative purpose, on the proposal of Stéphane Ndoumbe Ekale of the Ngondo Committee, under the Sawa traditional assembly. One source says authorities banned it in 1981.
Recognition: Recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. The first anniversary of that recognition was marked in December 2025.

title: Muna Moto
text:
Muna Moto (film)
Year: 1975 (some listings say 1974)
Director: Jean-Pierre Dikongué Pipa
Genre: Drama
Languages: French, Duala, Basaa
Running time: 89 minutes
Story: Ngando and Ndomé are in love, but Ngando must settle the traditional dowry with her family before he can marry her.
Honours: Won the Golden Stallion of Yennenga, the top prize of the Panafrican Film and Television Festival of Ouagadougou (FESPACO), in 1976. Official selection at the Venice Film Festival in 1975.
Significance: Described as Cameroon's first full-length feature film. A journal article names Point de Vue No. 1 as the first feature shot in Cameroon.
Release note: Released in Cameroonian cinemas in 1976 and was not a commercial success.

title: Bassek Ba Kobhio
text:
Bassek Ba Kobhio (public figure)
Born: 1 January 1957, in Nindjé, Ndom, Sanaga-Maritime Department (Littoral Region).
Died: In the night of 11 to 12 May 2026, in Yaoundé, aged 69, after an illness. Several outlets and the festival itself reported his death.
Occupations: Film director, producer and writer.
Film festival: Founded the Écrans Noirs festival in Yaoundé. The operation began in 1996 and the festival in 1997. He founded the Association Écrans Noirs in 2009, and it was recognised as being of public utility in 2016.
Films: Sango Malo (The Village Teacher, 1990 or 1991, adapted from his own novel), Le Grand Blanc de Lambaréné (1995, some lists say 1994, about Albert Schweitzer), the documentary Musique s'en va-t-en guerre (1997) and Le Silence de la forêt (2003, with Didier Ouénangaré).
Honours: Knight of the Burkina Faso National Order of Merit of the Arts (2009), Knight of the French Order of Arts and Letters (2013) and Knight of Cameroon's Order of Valour (2017).
Last project: He was preparing the 30th edition of Écrans Noirs when he died.

title: Jean-Pierre Bekolo
text:
Jean-Pierre Bekolo (public figure)
Born: 8 June 1966, in Yaoundé.
Training: Studied physics at the University of Yaoundé and trained in film editing at the Institut National de l'Audiovisuel in Paris, where he studied semiotics with Christian Metz.
First feature: Quartier Mozart (1992), shown at the Cannes Film Festival when he was 25.
Awards: A British Film Institute award in 1993 for Quartier Mozart. A special mention of the Holden Award for best script at Turin in 2005 and the Silver Étalon de Yennenga at FESPACO in 2007, both for Les Saignantes.
Films: Quartier Mozart (1992), Have You Seen Franklin Roosevelt? (1994), Aristotle's Plot (1996), La Grammaire de ma grand-mère (1996), Les Saignantes (2005), Imagine Afrika (2007), Le Président (2013), Les Choses et les Mots de Mudimbe (2015) and Naked Reality (2016).
Le president: His 2013 film Le Président, a fake documentary satirising leaders who cling to power, is described as banned in Cameroon in 2013.
Teaching: Has taught filmmaking at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and Duke University, and held a Harvard fellowship in 2023 to 2024.

title: Cameroonian literature
text:
Cameroonian literature (overview)
Languages: French, English and Cameroonian languages.
Colonial era: Writers such as Louis-Marie Pouka and Sankie Maimo were educated by European missionary societies and argued for assimilation into European culture.
After the second world war: Writers such as Mongo Beti and Ferdinand Oyono analysed and criticised colonialism and rejected assimilation.
First generation of novelists: Mongo Beti, René Philombe, Francis Bebey and Ferdinand Oyono, with a mission of close and critical analysis of colonisation.
Other older writers: Guillaume Oyono-Mbia, Mbella Sonne Dipoko and Kenjo Jumbam.
Critically acclaimed writers: Marcien Towa, Imbolo Mbue, Patrice Nganang, Calixthe Beyala, Bate Besong, Gaston-Paul Effa, Werewere Liking, Ba'bila Mutia, John Nkemngong Nkengasong, Bole Butake, Leonora Miano, Francis B. Nyamnjoh and Linus T. Asong.
Honour: Sankie Maimo received the Grand prix de la mémoire at the 2016 Grand Prix of Literary Associations (GPLA).

title: Mongo Beti
text:
Mongo Beti (public figure)
Real name: Alexandre Biyidi Awala
Pen names: Mongo Beti and Eza Boto
Born: 30 June 1932, in Mbalmayo
Died: 8 October 2001, in Douala
Language: French
Award: Prix Sainte-Beuve (1958).
Early writing: Sans haine et sans amour (1953), a short story, was his first significant writing.
Main themes: A commitment to fighting colonialism, open or hidden.
Main basse: He published Main basse sur le Cameroun in 1972. It was banned in France, and in 1976 he and his editor François Maspéro won its release through the courts.
Return: After 32 years of exile he returned to Cameroon and wrote La France contre l'Afrique, retour au Cameroun (1993).
Education: Studied at Aix-en-Provence and then at the Sorbonne in Paris, and took the agrégation in 1966.

title: Makossa
text:
Makossa (music genre)
Origin: Douala, in the 20th century. Sources differ on the exact decade.
Name meaning: Means (I) dance in the Douala language.
Roots: Grew out of the Douala kossa dance and drew on ambasse bey, assiko, highlife, Congolese rumba and merengue.
Early figures: Emmanuel Nelle Eyoum used the refrain kossa kossa with his group Los Calvinos. In the mid-1960s Eboa Lotin played an early form on harmonica and guitar.
Milestones: Had a wave of mainstream success across Africa in the 1980s. Manu Dibango's Soul Makossa came out in 1972. Shakira sampled the Golden Sounds song Zamina mina (Zangalewa) for the 2010 World Cup.
Related style: Makassi is a lighter style of makossa.

title: Bikutsi
text:
Bikutsi (music genre)
Origin: Centre Region, around Yaoundé, among the Beti (Ewondo) people.
Description: A native folk music based on a war rhythm, played by three to five balafon players with other percussion.
History: Migration to Yaoundé helped spread it. By the 1970s performers had added brass instruments and more explicit lyrics.
Notable group: Les Têtes Brulées became a well-known export, especially after accompanying the national football team to the 1990 and 1994 World Cups.
Relationship: Seen as a rival to the more urban makossa of Douala.

text:
Assiko (music genre)
Origin: A folk rhythm of the Bassa people.
Description: A local variant of palm wine music. Makossa can sound like a slowed-down assiko.
Styles: Hard, fast assiko among the Bassa and Eton, a cooler assiko among the Bulu, and the bottle dance of the Northwest Region.

title: Ambasse bey
text:
Ambasse bey (music genre)
Origin: Late 19th century, in German Kamerun. It began among the Yabassi people and became popular in Douala after the Second World War.
Description: Folk music and dance based on guitar, with sticks and bottles for percussion. It is faster than assiko.
Dance: Dancers wear traditional Sawa outfits.
Legacy: A precursor of makossa. Sallé John helped revive it.
Name variant: Also written ambas-i-bay.

title: Baka people
text:
Baka people (ethnic group)
Home: The rainforests of southeast Cameroon, in the South and East regions, and neighbouring Congo, the Central African Republic and Gabon.
Size: Estimates for Cameroon range from about 30,000 to about 40,000.
Way of life: Traditionally hunter-gatherers. During the twentieth century many began to settle and adopt agriculture.
Neighbours: They live alongside farming peoples such as the Njem.
Spirituality: The Baka honour the forest spirit Jengi (also written Djengui or Ejengi).
Knowledge: A deep knowledge of the forest, including the wild yam, which holds a central place in their cosmology between humans, elephants and forest spirits.
Terminology: The outsider term pygmy is criticised for suggesting primitiveness, so use Baka or the group's own name.

title: Baka polyphonic singing
text:
Baka polyphonic singing (music tradition)
Description: Vocal choirs in which several melodies are sung at the same time, with polyrhythmic percussion.
Roles: The singing is done by women, while the men march the song, meaning they dance.
Instruments: Baka music is essentially vocal, and instruments accompany the singing.
Meaning: Singing and dancing are linked to the forest spirits and the ancestors.
Recording: Smithsonian Folkways reissued the album Cameroon: Baka Pygmy Music in its UNESCO Collection of Traditional Music.
Caution: One website says Baka polyphony is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list. That listing refers to the Aka people of the Central African Republic and Congo, so it is not recorded here for the Baka.

title: Mvet
text:
Mvet (instrument)
Description: A double-sided harp with calabash amplification, used by Beti storytellers.
Role: The storytellers are viewed as using the mvet as an instrument of God to educate the people.
Setting: Played at Beti gatherings such as parties, funerals and weddings.

title: Ekang and bikutsi phases of Beti gatherings
text:
Ekang and bikutsi phases of Beti gatherings (tradition)
Ekang phase: The time when imaginary, mythological and spiritual issues are discussed. It is intensely musical, usually lasts all night, and has poetic recitations with clapping and dancing.
Balafon: Interludes of improvised, sometimes obscene balafon playing signal the shift to the bikutsi phase.
Bikutsi phase: Much less strictly structured. Women dance and sing along with the balafon, and the lyrics deal with real-life problems.
Rhythm: Bikutsi is characterised by an intense 6/8 rhythm.
Balafon orchestras: Balafon orchestras of three to five balafons with percussion became common in bars.

title: Bamenda Grassfields
text:
Bamenda Grassfields (region)
Where: The Northwest Region and the surrounding grassland areas, with the West Region.
Name: The Germans first used the term grassfields for the Bamenda highlands, which differ from the coastal forest.
Peoples: Mainly the Tikar, Bamileke, Bamum, Ngemba, Widikum and Ngie groups, with Chamba-derived Bali chiefdoms.
Centralised fondoms: Kom (Bikom), Bafut, Nso and Bali are the main centralised fondoms the colonial authorities met.
Tikar share: In one study area the Tikar were about 60% of the population, represented by Nso', Oku, Mbum, Kom, Bafut, Yamba and Aghem.
Terminology: A Fon rules a fondom, in the way a king rules a kingdom.

title: Fon (title)
text:
Fon (title) (title)
Meaning: A chieftain or king of a region of Cameroon, especially among the Ngie, Widikum, Tikar and Bamileke peoples of the Bamenda Grassfields (Northwest and West regions) and in Lebialem in the Southwest Region.
Local words for king: Mfon in Mungaka, Ibyn in Kom, Ilon in Lamnso' and Ilo in Ngemba.
Examples: Fons of Bafut, Nso, Bali Nyonga, Mankon, Oku, Bafanji and Fontem.
Southwest note: In the Southwest Region only Lebialem Division has Fons, the best known being the Fon of Fontem.

title: Bafut kingdom
text:
Bafut kingdom (kingdom)
Location: About 20 km northwest of Bamenda, in Mezam Department, Northwest Region.
Size: About 340 square kilometres, with 80,000 people in 2005, in 26 wards along 10 km of the Ring Road.
Status: Traditionally the most powerful of the Grassfields kingdoms, whose Fons were paramount over many neighbours.
Palace: The palace of the Fon of Bafut houses a museum.
Festival: The annual festival Abin e Mfor (the dance of the Fon).
Council: The Fon shared power with a council of elders called the Kwifor, restricted to commoners who had reached the rank of Bukum. It acted as kingmaker and a check on royal power.
German period: In 1891 Bafut helped its neighbour Mankon, which was attacked by a German-led Bali Nyonga force. Relations with the Germans then worsened into the Bafut Wars of the early 20th century.
Language: Bafut, a Mbam-Nkam language, and Cameroon Pidgin English.

title: Bali Nyonga
text:
Bali Nyonga (kingdom)
Origin: A Chamba Leko group that migrated from the Chamba area of northern Cameroon to the Bamenda Grassfields, mixing Western Grassfields, southern Bamum and Chamba elements.
Palace: Galega I moved the palace to the present capital in about 1875.
German period: An early ally of the German colonial forces, which strengthened its chiefs against other Grassfields chiefdoms.
Name: Fonyonga means the Fon of the Nyonga people.

title: Kwifor
text:
Kwifor (council)
Description: A council of elders in Grassfields kingdoms such as Bafut, whose members acted as kingmakers and a check on the Fon's power.
Bafut rule: Membership was restricted to commoners who had reached the rank of Bukum.
Related societies: In Nso a comparable regulatory society is the Ngwerong. Regulatory associations are called Kwi'fon in the Bum chiefdom.

title: Nso (Banso) people
text:
Nso (Banso) people (people)
Other names: Banso, Bansaw, Bansso, Banzo, Nsaw, Lamnso (also used for the language). The Nso' take their name from their founder Ngonnso'.
Home: The Bamenda Grassfields in the Northwest Region, mainly Bui Division.
Capital: Kumbo (also called Kimbo), where the Fon's palace stands.
Language: Lamnso' (Nso).
Size: Estimates differ. About 240,000 speakers of Lamnso' (2005 estimate), about 217,000 people on 2,300 square kilometres in one source, and 401,000 Nso in Cameroon in a Joshua Project profile.
Standing: Described as the largest ethnic group of the Northwest Region.
Classification: Considered a subgroup of the Tikar by one reference.
Ba prefix: Banso means people of Nso. Sources disagree on the Ba- prefix: one attributes it to Fulani conquerors in the 17th century, another says such forms came from foreign influence.
Economy: An agricultural society. Women are the farmers and are called the backbone of the country. Men owned the fields while women owned the crops.
Languages in use: Lamnso', Cameroon Pidgin English, English, Limbum and Oku.

title: Nso' kingdom
text:
Nso' kingdom (kingdom)
Capital: Kumbo
Political head: The Fon.
Area: Nso', Oku and Mbiame together form Bui Division.
Bui division 1976: About 142,000 people, in an area roughly like that of Luxembourg.
Other fons: Other Fons act as advisers to the Fon of Nso. Most were once leaders of independent groups that came under the Fon of Nso through war, peaceful agreement or events of history. The Fons of Oku and Mbiame were once princes of Nso.
Tikar dynasties: Nso, Kom, Bafut, Bum and Ndu were five kingdoms with Tikar or Ndobo-derived dynasties that grew in the nineteenth century.

title: Origin and migration of the Nso
text:
Origin and migration of the Nso (history)
Origin: The Nso' came from Tikari, in the Adamawa area, after a bloody succession dispute following the death of Chief Tinki in 1387, according to one source.
Leader: Ngonnso', founder of the Nso' dynasty, left Kimi with a few followers and her brothers Nchare Yen and Mbombam with their followers.
Bamum link: Her brother Nchare Yen is named as the eventual founder of the Bamum kingdom.
Route: After parting from her brothers, Ngonnso' and her followers settled successively at Mbo'nso', Ndzennso' and Kovifem, withdrew to Taavisa for security, returned to Kovifem and finally moved to Kimbo (Kumbo).
First german contact: Lieutenant Kurt von Pavel's first contact with the Nso' was friendly, and he received a ram from the Fon.

title: Ngonnso'
text:
Ngonnso' (public figure)
Role: Founder of the Nso' dynasty and first queen mother of the Nso kingdom, revered as a mother deity.
Name meaning: Means young lady of Nso, according to Quartz.
Legend: She left a succession conflict with her brothers Nchare Yen and Mbombam and led her followers to Kumbo.
Statue: The statue that represents her was taken in colonial times and is now in Berlin.

title: Fon of Nso
text:
Fon of Nso (office)
Role: Head of the traditional government and the chief religious authority, in charge of keeping the ancestors happy.
Seat: The palace in Kumbo.
Name: Sehm Mbinglo I is named as the Fon in several Wikipedia articles and photo captions, while one passage says Sehm Mbinglo II as of 2013.
Earlier fon: Fon Ngah Bifon I reigned from 1910 to 1947.
Limits: His power is checked by regulatory societies such as the Ngwerong.
Caution: Check who holds the office now, because the sources date from 2013 or earlier.

title: Ngwerong
text:
Ngwerong (society)
Also spelled: Nwerong
Role: A regulatory society that is in effect the security arm of the government and enforces the decisions of the Fon.
Enthronement: It alone is responsible for the enthronement of a new Fon.
Members: All the Fons of Nso and Shufai Ndzendzev belong to both the Ngwerong and the Ngiri.
Masked spirits: Ngwerong and Ngiri each have seven jujus, often seen on the way to a member's death celebration.

Description: The princes' society of the Nso.
Members: The Fons of Nso and Shufai Ndzendzev belong to it and to the Ngwerong.

title: Fai and Shey
text:
Fai and Shey (concept)
Fai: A leader of a lineage group. Nso society is divided into groups by lineage, each led by a Fai who is instituted by the Fon.
Etiquette: Tradition says a Fai's hand is not shaken.
Appearance: Fais are recognised by glass bead necklaces and fancy walking sticks.
Shey: Other leaders called Sheys are a level below the Fais.
Princes: Princes are called Wontho and meet in the presence of the Fon to discuss family matters.

text:
Jujus of the Nso (concept)
Description: Jujus are masked spirits and an important part of Nso culture.
Occasions: They come out on important occasions, and the passing of a juju led by its handlers and followed by children is a street performance.
Music: Other jujus are groups that dance to drums and xylophones. Music and the skilful use of traditional melodies are central to Nso culture.

Ngam Ngonnso cultural week (festival)
Also called: Ngonnso Cultural Festival
Place: Kumbo
Description: A cultural week that brings together the traditions of the Nso and neighbouring peoples, with jujus on display from the palace to the other quarters of Kumbo.
Attendance: Tens of thousands of people attend the multi-day festival every year, according to a news feature on Ngonnso'.

Kilankenyuy (myth)
Meaning: In Lamnso' it means the stone of God.
Role: The name the Nso give to the God who gives children.

title: Kumbo
text:
Kumbo (town)
Role: Capital of the Nso kingdom and the seat of the Fon.
Palace: The Nso Palace is the heart of the town's social and cultural life.
Market: The Mbve market is the main market, selling products from the region, Cameroon, Nigeria and elsewhere.
Known for: Horse racing (Tobin Stadium), traditional medicine, the palace and two hospitals, Shisong Hospital and Banso Baptist Hospital.
Statue: A statue of Ngonnso', the legendary first queen of the Nso, stands in the palace compound. It is a replica made in 2008, since the original is in Berlin.
Former name: Kimbo

Location: The Kumbo area, in Nso country.
Services: Hosts a nursing school, a network of clinics, an HIV management programme and a surgical residency.

Collection: Includes utensils made by the Grassfields peoples of the Northwest and West.

title: Peoples of Cameroon
text:
Peoples of Cameroon (overview)
Number: About 250 ethnic groups. Cameroon likes to call itself Africa in miniature.
Five groups: Often grouped into five regional-cultural divisions: western highlanders or Grassfielders (Bamileke, Bamoun, Tikar), about 38%; southern tropical forest peoples (Ewondo, Bulu and Fang, who are Beti subgroups, plus Maka and Baka), about 18%; coastal tropical forest peoples (Bassa, Duala and others), about 12%; the predominantly Muslim peoples of the Sahel and central highlands (Fulani), about 14%; and the Kirdi, about 18%. These shares are older estimates.
World factbook categories: A 2022 estimate reported by EBSCO gives: Bamileke-Bamu 22.2%, Beti/Bassa/Mbam 13.1%, Biu-Mandara 16.4%, Arab-Choa/Hausa/Kanuri 13.5%, Adamawa-Ubangi 9.8%, Grassfields 9.9%, Kako/Meka/Pygmy 2.3%, Cotier/Ngoe/Oroko 4.6% and Southwestern Bantu 4.3%.
Caution: Estimates differ between sources and years, and none comes from a recent census.
Population: 29,321,637 (2022 estimate).

title: Bamileke
text:
Bamileke (ethnic group)
Home: The western highlands, in the West and Northwest regions.
Languages: Variants of Ghomala', Fe'fe', Yemba, Medumba and Kwa.
Government: Traditionally patriarchal and hereditary, under Fons.
Economy: Agriculture is mainly done by women. Bamileke are entrepreneurial, are found in almost all parts of Cameroon, and form much of the business community in coastal towns.
Culture: Known for the ndop cloth.

title: Beti-Pahuin
text:
Beti-Pahuin (ethnic group)
Home: The southern rainforest regions.
Subgroups: Ewondo, Bulu and Fang, with the related Maka, Njem and Baka.
History: Served as middlemen in the European trade. Some groups were displaced by the Fulani jihad, and the Germans used them for forced labour and road building.
Economy: A strong economic influence through cocoa farming.
Language: Ewondo, the dialect of a Beti clan from the Yaoundé area, has wide currency across the country.

title: Duala (Sawa) and Bassa
text:
Duala (Sawa) and Bassa (ethnic group)
Home: The coastal tropical forest, including Douala, and the Southwest.
Groups: The Duala, the Bassa and many smaller groups, together about 12% of the population in older estimates.
Traditions: The Sawa peoples celebrate the Ngondo festival and wear the kaba ngondo. Makossa originated in Douala, ambasse bey became popular there, and assiko is a Bassa rhythm.
Politics: The nationalist party UPC was based largely among the Bamileke and Bassa.

title: Fulani (Fulbe)
text:
Fulani (Fulbe) (ethnic group)
Share: About 14% of the population in older estimates.
Religion: Muslim, with a culture strongly influenced by Islamic practice.
Language: Fulfulde.
History: The Fulani conquered most of what is now northern Cameroon between the late 1770s and early 1800s, subjugating or displacing its largely non-Muslim people.
North: In the Adamawa, North and Far North regions French and Fulfulde are widely spoken.
Title: Rulers in the north are called Lamido.

title: Kirdi
text:
Kirdi (ethnic group)
Description: A name for the non-Islamic or recently Islamic peoples of the northern desert and central highlands, about 18% of the population in older estimates.
Origin of term: The word was used by outsiders for people who refused to join Islam.
Languages: Chadic and Adamawa languages.
Caution: Treat the term with care, since it comes from outsiders and covers many different peoples.

title: Tikar
text:
Tikar (ethnic group)
Description: A group of peoples whose dynasties founded many Grassfields kingdoms.
Kingdoms: Nso, Kom, Bafut, Bum and Ndu had Tikar or Ndobo-derived dynasties. The Bamum founder Nshare Yèn is called a Tikar prince.
Size: The largest of three groups in one Grassfields study, about 60% of the population there.
Nso: One reference considers the Nso a subgroup of the Tikar.

title: Cameroon Pidgin English
text:
Cameroon Pidgin English (language)
Also called: Kamtok
Iso 639 3: wes
Description: An English-based pidgin that serves as a language of wider communication across Cameroon.
Status: Less prestigious than English and French, but felt to be more African than either. It has no official status.
Regional languages: About 7 or 8 indigenous languages and Cameroon Pidgin English have become regional lingua francas.
Speakers: The number of speakers is hard to determine because they range from first-language and fluent second-language speakers to people who use it only occasionally.
Grammar note: Nouns do not change for number or gender.
Old data: A 1983 study found Pidgin as a first language for 22% of the people in Bamenda, 25% in Mamfe, 19% in Kumba, 26% in Buea and 31% in Limbe.

title: Camfranglais
text:
Camfranglais (language)
Names: Camfranglais (from camerounais, français and anglais), also called Francanglais.
Description: A highly mixed urban youth speech made of Cameroonian French, Cameroonian English and Cameroon Pidgin English, with words from indigenous languages.
Where: Mainly the big cities of Yaoundé and Douala.
Speakers: Mostly young people aged 12 to 26, and mostly male, though more young women are using it.
Writing: Written Camfranglais shows a strong tendency to make words from Duala, Ewondo, Basaa and Mokpe look French.
Purpose: A way for youth to form a modern urban identity separate from French, English and indigenous languages.
Concerns: Some educators worry it may hinder learning of standard French and English.
Codes: It has no ISO 639-3 code. Glottolog uses camf1234.

title: Lamnso'
text:
Lamnso' (language)
Also called: Nso, Nsɔ, Lamnsɔ'
Iso 639 3: lns
Glottolog: lamn1239
Speakers: 240,000 in Cameroon (2005 estimate). Another source says over 100,000.
Family: A Grassfields language of the Ring group (Niger-Congo, Southern Bantoid).
Grammar: Has ten major noun classes.
Region: Bui Division, in the Northwest Region.
Other languages used: Cameroon Pidgin English, English, Limbum and Oku.
Writing: Written since the 1940s, when Nso schoolteachers developed a spelling system on their own initiative to teach primary school pupils in their own language before they moved on to English.
Bible: The Bible translation began in 1971. The New Testament was available for many years, and the complete Bible was dedicated in November 2016, together with a Lamnso' dictionary.
References: Anderson, S. C. (2015), A phonological sketch of Lamnso', SIL Cameroon. McGarrity and Botne (2001), Between agreement and case marking in Lamnso.

title: Official languages clause of the 1996 Constitution
text:
Official languages clause of the 1996 Constitution (law)
Article: Section 1, Article 1, paragraph 3 of the 1996 Constitution.
Content: The official languages of Cameroon are English and French, both having the same status. The State guarantees the promotion of bilingualism throughout the country and endeavours to protect and promote the national languages.
Criticism: Scholars note that this does not give any indigenous language official status, and that French is far more visible in public space than English.
Note: Summarised from scholarly papers that quote the clause.

title: Njangi (tontine)
text:
Njangi (tontine) (institution)
Description: A rotating savings and credit association (ROSCA) in which members pool money at agreed, regular intervals and each member receives the pot in turn.
Names: Njangi among Anglophone Cameroonians and tontine among Francophones. Other names for the same idea elsewhere include esusu in Nigeria.
Language: Members say they play njangi, and the member who receives the money is said to chop njangi, although they are expected to invest it wisely and not waste it.
Saying: A well-known saying is life na njangi, meaning life is give and take.
Rules: Each njangi has its own rules, and trust and shared values among members are important.
Purpose: Savings, loans and social support, including paying school fees, in places where banks are scarce or distant.
Loan effect: A member who receives early gets what is in effect an interest-free loan, and one who receives late uses it as savings.
Bamileke: The Bamileke of the Western Region use these associations extensively to finance small businesses, using names such as tontine, njangi and Ntshwa.
Technology: A study of mobile money found that electronic money was making njangi transactions more secure.
Origin of word tontine: The French word is said to come from the Italian banker Lorenzo Tonti, who suggested a mutual insurance scheme in the 17th century.

title: Hometown associations of the Bamileke in Yaoundé
text:
Hometown associations of the Bamileke in Yaoundé (institution)
Description: Associations of people from the same home area living in a city, in this study Bamileke women from Ndé Division living in Yaoundé.
Kinds: Elite associations, whose members are urbanites with diverse social networks and a universal language about bringing development to the hometown, and non-elite neighbourhood associations, which resemble dense urban villages that try to bring home to the city.
Meaning: They help members feel they belong, and emotions of memory, marginalisation and recognition shape what home means.
Source type: An academic study published in the journal Africa.

Nickname: The Indomitable Lions (Les Lions Indomptables)
Governing body: Fédération Camerounaise de Football

Olympics: Won the men's Olympic football gold medal in Sydney in 2000.
Most popular sport: Football is the most popular sport in Cameroon.
